Proposed: The pilot workload specification separates the event capture timestamp from receiver observation time. The design review must retain this distinction even when explaining the system to an executive audience.

A failure report would identify invalid item indexes and fixed error classes without echoing temperatures, raw payloads, secrets, or authentication headers. No invalid batch would be partially acknowledged, and no rejected item would acquire a success receipt.

Proposed: The proposed duplicate check compares the previously stored canonical reading payload with the incoming payload under the trusted principal and sequence key. A changed payload under an existing key would remain a conflict even if its timestamp is newer. The conflict path would neither overwrite history nor claim that the new reading was accepted. Proposed: The proposed append protocol would write a complete batch record with its validation outcome and duplicate receipt material before acknowledging success. Replay would rebuild both the data index and retry receipts from that durable record. Acknowledgment would wait for the configured durability barrier; a successful append system call alone would not establish durable completion. If the barrier or response fails after append, the receiver would preserve uncertainty and require exact retry or investigation. This proposal has not been measured against real disks.

The proposed safe default is to stop intake at any ambiguous tail and preserve the original bytes for investigation. Automated truncation, deletion, or reconstruction would not follow merely from a parse error. Any future repair tool would need its own exact scope, authorization and replay evidence. The pilot would report the last verified position separately from the number of bytes that happen to exist in the log.

Proposed: The proposed test report would state independently expected acknowledged batch IDs, recovered batch IDs, duplicate response comparisons, deliberately conflicting submissions and every injected interruption point. Expected IDs would come from the fixture author rather than the receiver output. A missing receipt, skipped restart, incomplete log inspection or unobserved durability barrier would be an unknown result, not a pass. The report would separate correctness from observed latency and storage consumption. Repeating one replay would not establish independent production reliability.

Proposed: Observability review would compare fixed counters with the fixture manifest after the run, including malformed requests rejected before record parsing and storage outcomes that remained uncertain. A counter source that did not exist or stopped reporting would be a coverage gap. Batch correlation values would be used only for the synthetic exercise and would not imply permission to log arbitrary caller text in production. The proposed alert threshold remains a tuning hypothesis; no alert volume, response-time improvement or operational cost saving has been measured.

Proposed: Before implementation, the design owner would need to select and record the finite disk quota, retention behavior, full-disk response, segment rotation policy, canonical payload encoding and supported operating system. A 64 MiB rotation suggestion is not a total storage budget and does not settle retention. The isolated pilot could not admit production traffic while those prerequisites remain unresolved. Any later decision would create a new design revision and require the affected recovery and capacity cases to be rerun rather than inheriting a previous result.
